newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Forestry Corp NZ re-nationalisation seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Forestry Corp NZ re-nationalisation seen unlikely.

text.p: Re-nationalisation of the former state-owned Forestry Corp of New Zealand Ltd (FCNZ) after the October 12 general election was unlikely, political and industry analysts said on Friday.

FCNZ, controversially sold in August to a consortium comprising Fletcher Challenge Forests, Brierley Investments Ltd and China's Citic, has become a political football, with the economic nationalist NZ First and the leftist Alliance parties pledging its return to the state.
NZ First has said the NZ$1.6 billion cheque would simply be returned to the buyers while the Alliance has embarked on a signature campaign to call for a referendum on the issue.

The Labour Party has said it would not nationalise the asset but Forestry Minister John Falloon says the centre-left Labour "could not resist the temptation", particularly if it formed a coalition with NZ First and the Alliance.

"There is a grave risk that the extreme polices of the Alliance and New Zealand First will do irreparable harm to investment in forestry," Falloon said in a recent statement. "For a government to legislate the buy-back of a forest that was going to be sold as logs anyway is stupidity," Falloon said.
At stake are cutting rights to 188,000 hectares of plantation forests in the central North Island.

Raymond Miller, political studies lecturer at Auckland University, said Labour had given NZ First an apparent face-saving opportunity by suggesting other parties could introduce legislation to parliament.

"What Labour has indicated is that there are certain things that they would be happy for other parties to introduce in parliament to see how they get on with them, and I think the forestry one is one of those.

"But Labour would feel that it certainly would not be prepared to make that an issue which determined the future of a coalition. In other words, Labour feels that it would undermine the country's commercial credibility if they did anything with the sale at this point."
Miller said in its approach to the sale of Forestry Corp, along with other economic issues, Labour had distanced itself from the other opposition parties.
"Labour has made it very clear that on social policy issues there was room for considerable accommodation, but not on certain economic issues," Miller said.

He said if the Alliance got enough support, a referendum could follow. "But by that stage it would become something of an irrelevance and I would doubt if there would be enough public support at that point."
Referenda take between 12-18 months to organise.
Graham Hall, National Secretary of the New Zealand Forest Owners' Association, said the arguments were sound as to why a return of the asset to the state should not happen.
"After all, the trees were grown to be sold sooner or later, and it's a question of whether they are sold upright or lying down," Hall said.
A recent opinion poll showed Labour had finally cemented itself in the number two position. The poll said National had 37 percent support, Labour 21, NZ First 16 and the Alliance 11.
